name: Repetition code memory (bit-flip)
summary: Monte Carlo logical error rate of the n-qubit bit-flip repetition code under i.i.d. bit flips, beside the exact binomial value.
description:
Runs a memory experiment of the bit-flip repetition code on your machine. Each of the n data qubits flips independently with probability p; the Z_i Z_{i+1} syndrome is extracted (perfectly) and decoded by minimum weight, which for this code is majority vote; the logical qubit fails when the correction differs from the error, that is when more than n/2 qubits flipped. The product samples this with a seed and reports the logical error rate with a 95% Wilson score interval.

What makes this product useful as a reference is that the answer is known exactly: P_L = sum over k > n/2 of C(n, k) p^k (1-p)^(n-k). The exact value is reported beside the Monte Carlo estimate, together with whether it lies inside the interval, so you can see a sampling experiment and its closed form on the same output.

For students meeting error correction for the first time, and as a sanity baseline for anyone building a Monte Carlo pipeline for larger codes.
useCases: Watch the logical error rate fall with n below the pseudo-threshold p = 1/2 and rise above it
Check a Monte Carlo pipeline (sampling, decoding, confidence intervals) against an exact closed form
Produce a seeded, reproducible memory-experiment record with a Wilson interval for a chosen (n, p, shots)

inputs.name: n
inputs.description: Number of data qubits (the code distance). Odd, so that majority vote is defined.

inputs.name: physical_error_rate
inputs.description: Bit-flip probability p applied independently to each qubit.

inputs.name: shots
inputs.description: Number of sampled experiments. n x shots above 10^9 is refused with the time estimate.

outputs.name: logical_failures
outputs.description: Shots whose decoded correction left the logical qubit flipped.

outputs.name: confidence_interval
outputs.description: 95% Wilson score interval: lower, upper, level, method.

outputs.name: exact_logical_error_rate
outputs.description: sum_{k > n/2} C(n, k) p^k (1-p)^(n-k), the closed form the estimate is compared with.

outputs.name: exact_within_interval
outputs.description: Whether the exact value lies inside the Wilson interval.

outputs.name: is_upper_bound_only
outputs.description: true when no failure was observed; then only the upper bound is meaningful.

changes: First catalog release: NumPy Monte Carlo of the bit-flip repetition code with syndrome decoding, Wilson interval and exact binomial reference.

environment.resources: n=3 with 10^4 shots: milliseconds. 10^8 sampled qubit flips (for example n=11 with 10^7 shots): ~1.5 s and under 100 MB on a 2024 laptop; shots are processed in fixed chunks so memory stays bounded. n x shots above 10^9 (~15 s) is refused.

example.code:
import json
from ketqat_runner import catalog

record = catalog.run("repetition-code@1.0.0", seed=7, n=5, physical_error_rate=0.1, shots=20000)
result = record.result
interval = result["confidence_interval"]
print(json.dumps({
    "status": record.status,
    "n": result["n"],
    "exact_logical_error_rate": round(result["exact_logical_error_rate"], 9),
    "exact_within_interval": result["exact_within_interval"],
    "interval_brackets_rate": interval["lower"] <= result["logical_error_rate"] <= interval["upper"],
    "below_pseudothreshold": result["below_pseudothreshold"],
}))

verified.platform: macOS-27.0.1-arm64 Python 3.12.12 (maintainer run in a clean virtualenv, test_catalog_examples.py)

sampleResult.summary: n = 3 at p = 0.1 with 10000 shots: 252 logical failures, rate 0.0252 with 95% Wilson interval [0.0223, 0.0285], which contains the exact value 3p^2 - 2p^3 = 0.028; below the pseudo-threshold, since 0.028 < 0.1.

data.noise_model: independent bit flip with probability p on each data qubit, one round, perfect syndrome measurement
data.decoder: majority vote (minimum-weight correction from the Z_i Z_{i+1} syndrome)
data.exact_formula: sum_{k > n/2} C(n, k) p^k (1 - p)^(n - k)
data.execution: seeded NumPy Monte Carlo of per-qubit bit flips, syndrome extraction and majority-vote decoding

assumptions: Independent, identically distributed bit flips (X errors) with probability p on each data qubit, applied once.
Perfect syndrome measurement and a single round: no measurement errors, no idling errors and no repeated extraction.
Minimum-weight decoding from the Z_i Z_{i+1} syndrome, which equals majority vote for this code; the decoder is cross-checked against a direct majority vote on every chunk.
scope: Odd n from 1 to 101 and any p in [0, 1]; up to 10^9 sampled qubit flips per run.
Logical error rate per experiment with a 95% Wilson score interval and the exact binomial value.
limitations: A bit-flip code protects against X errors only; phase flips are not modelled and the code would not correct them.
No circuit-level noise, no measurement errors and no multi-round memory: the rate is per single round with perfect syndromes, which is why it has a closed form.
Zero observed failures is reported as an upper bound, not as a rate of zero; at small p and small shot counts the interval is wide.
Sampled counts are reproducible for the same seed with the same NumPy version; NumPy does not guarantee identical random streams across versions.
Tested on macOS and Linux only; Windows is untested.

origin.statement: The majority-vote repetition code is classical coding theory going back to Hamming (1950); its quantum bit-flip form is the textbook three-qubit code treated by Nielsen and Chuang, and Shor (1995) used it as a building block of the first quantum error-correcting code. The Wilson score interval is due to Wilson (1927). KetQat wrote this NumPy Monte Carlo implementation (repetition_code.py), its syndrome decoder, the exact reference, the validation tests and this catalog entry. KetQat did not invent the code.

validation.description: For (n, p) in {(1, 0.1), (3, 0.1), (5, 0.1), (7, 0.2), (9, 0.05), (3, 0.3)} with 20000 seeded shots, the Wilson interval around the Monte Carlo rate contains the exact binomial tail, recomputed in the test with math.comb; for n = 1 the exact rate is p itself.
p = 0 gives zero failures, exact rate 0 and an upper-bound-only report; p = 1 flips every qubit, so every shot fails and both rates are exactly 1; p = 1/2 gives exact rate 1/2 for every odd n.
The syndrome-based decoder's failure count equals a direct majority vote on the same sampled flips, and both equal the count of shots with more than n/2 flips, on random flip tables.
Even n is refused, and n x shots above 10^9 is refused with the time estimate before anything runs.
The example code is executed verbatim in a clean virtual environment with only the qinfo extra installed.
